title: Processes and Threads
objectives: Say what a process owns and what its threads share
Explain what fork and exec each do
Choose processes or threads for isolation versus cheap sharing

cards.title: A process is a container for a running program
cards.body: A process owns an address space (its memory), open file descriptors, credentials and at least one thread of execution. The kernel keeps these apart, so one process cannot read another’s memory unless both deliberately share it. A crash in one process normally leaves the others running.

cards.title: Threads share almost everything
cards.body: Threads are separate paths of execution inside one process. Each has its own stack, registers and program counter, but all share the heap, global data and open files. That makes passing data between threads cheap and also makes it easy for one thread to corrupt data another is using.

cards.title: Worked example: starting a program with fork and exec
cards.body: Unix-like systems create processes in two steps.
steps: The shell calls fork: the kernel creates a child process that is a copy of the parent, sharing memory pages copy-on-write
fork returns twice: the child’s process id to the parent and 0 to the child
The child calls exec with the program path: its memory is replaced by the new program, while open file descriptors (unless marked close-on-exec) stay
The parent calls wait to collect the child’s exit status
If the parent never waits, the finished child stays as a “zombie” entry in the process table

cards.title: Misconception: threads are always lighter, so always better
cards.body: Threads avoid copying address spaces and switch a little faster, but sharing memory means a bug in any thread can corrupt the whole process and a crash takes every thread down. Processes cost more memory but isolate failures and can run with different permissions, which is why browsers and many servers use several processes.

cards.title: Trap: copy-on-write makes fork look free
cards.body: fork does not copy memory straight away: parent and child share every page, marked copy-on-write, and a page is copied only when one side writes to it. A child that calls exec at once costs little. A large process that forks a long-lived child, for example to write a snapshot, pays for a copy of every page it keeps writing: a 10 GB process that rewrites half its heap during the child’s life needs about 5 GB more memory, enough to trigger an out-of-memory kill.

cards.title: Edge case: fork in a multithreaded program
cards.body: fork copies the whole address space but only the thread that called it. If another thread held a lock at that moment, such as the memory allocator’s, the child inherits the lock in its held state with no thread to release it, and can hang on its next allocation. POSIX allows only async-signal-safe calls in the child of a multithreaded fork until it calls exec; prefer posix_spawn or spawning before starting threads.

questions.prompt: Two threads in one process both read a global variable. What does each see?

choices.label: The same memory location
A copy held in each core’s cache until a lock is taken
A copy-on-write page per thread
A private copy made at thread start

questions.explanation: Threads share one address space, so a global is one memory location for all of them; only stacks and registers are per thread. Caches are kept coherent by hardware, so there is no private per-core copy to sync (ordering still needs locks or atomics). Copy-on-write applies between processes after fork, and threads never get a private copy at start.

questions.prompt: What does exec do to the calling process?

choices.label: Replaces its program image
Starts a thread in the same process
Creates a new child process
Closes every open file descriptor

questions.explanation: exec keeps the process id but loads a new program; fork is what creates the process.

questions.prompt: A plugin with a history of crashes must not take the main app down. What is the safer home for it?

choices.label: A separate thread in the app
A thread with its own exception handler
A higher scheduling priority
A separate process

questions.explanation: A separate process has its own address space, so a crash or memory corruption in the plugin cannot reach the main app. A thread shares the address space: a segmentation fault ends the whole process, and an exception handler cannot catch memory corruption or a crash in native code. Scheduling priority changes when code runs, not what a crash takes down.

questions.prompt: A parent never calls wait on its finished children. What accumulates?

choices.label: Orphaned memory pages
Leaked threads in the parent
Open sockets in the child
Zombie process table entries

questions.explanation: A zombie keeps its exit status until the parent collects it.

questions.prompt: Order how a shell runs a command.

items.label: fork a child process
The parent waits and collects the exit status
exec the program in the child
The program runs and exits

questions.explanation: Create, replace, run, reap.

questions.prompt: An image-conversion service runs third-party decoders that occasionally crash on malformed files.
constraints: A crash must not drop other users’ requests

approaches.label: Run decoders inside each request handler
One process with a thread per conversion

rationaleOptions.label: Each worker can run with fewer permissions
Threads isolate crashes just as well
Processes cannot use several CPU cores
A decoder crash kills only one worker, which is restarted

rationaleConflicts.r3: A segmentation fault in one thread terminates the whole process.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Separate processes run on separate cores like threads do.

questions.explanation: A segmentation fault in a decoder kills whatever process it runs in, so only separate worker processes keep other users’ requests alive, and each worker can run with fewer permissions. Running inline or on threads shares one process, so one bad file drops everyone. Processes still use every core, and copying a file to a worker costs little next to a CPU-heavy conversion.

flashcards.back: An address space, file descriptors, credentials and one or more threads.

flashcards.front: What do threads in one process share?
flashcards.back: Heap, globals and open files; each has its own stack and registers.
fork copies the process; exec replaces the program in it.

mechanism.title: How the kernel represents processes and threads
steps: The kernel keeps a record for each process: its memory map, open file table, current directory, user and group ids, signal handlers and resource limits. Each process gets a process id (PID), and every process except the first has a parent.

A thread is the unit the scheduler runs. On Linux both processes and threads are created with clone; flags decide what the new task shares with its creator (memory, file table, signal handlers). A “process” is a group of tasks sharing one address space.

fork creates a child whose memory is a copy of the parent’s, but the copy is lazy: pages are shared read-only and copied only when one side writes (copy-on-write). That is why forking a large process is fast until both sides start writing.

exec loads a new program into the current process: new code, data, heap and stack, same PID. File descriptors stay open across exec unless they carry the close-on-exec flag, which is a common source of leaked descriptors in child programs.

When a process exits, the kernel keeps a small entry with its exit status until the parent reads it with wait. If the parent exits first, the child is re-parented to an init-like process that reaps it.

Choosing between them: threads suit work that shares large data structures and needs fast communication; processes suit isolation, different privileges and crash containment. Many servers combine both: a few processes, each with a pool of threads or an event loop.

useWhen: Use processes to isolate untrusted or crash-prone code and to drop privileges.
Use threads when tasks share large in-memory data and need cheap communication.
avoidWhen: Avoid forking a multi-threaded process and doing real work in the child before exec.
Avoid assuming a crash in one thread leaves the others running.

numbers.title: What copy-on-write saves when forking a large process
assumptions: A parent process uses 2 GB of memory in 4 KB pages (illustrative)
The child calls exec almost immediately
steps: 2 GB ÷ 4 KB ≈ 524,000 pages would need copying with an eager fork.
With copy-on-write, fork copies only page tables and marks pages read-only; almost no data is copied.
The child execs at once, so its shared mappings are dropped before either side writes much.
If instead both keep running and the parent rewrites 25% of its pages, about 131,000 pages (≈ 512 MB) are copied over time.
numbers.result: Copy-on-write makes fork-then-exec cheap, but a long-lived forked child that shares a write-heavy parent slowly duplicates its memory.

india.title: Copy-on-write snapshots in an in-memory store
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Redis documents that its RDB persistence forks the server process and lets the child write a snapshot while the parent keeps serving. Because of copy-on-write the child initially shares all memory, but every page the parent modifies during the snapshot is duplicated, so a write-heavy instance can need noticeably more memory while saving. The same effect appears whenever a long-running process forks a helper.

pitfalls.trap: “Threads are faster, so we run every plugin in a thread.”
pitfalls.say: “Threads are cheaper, but a crashing plugin would take the whole process down; I’d isolate it in a worker process.”

pitfalls.trap: “fork copies all memory, so it is too slow.”
pitfalls.say: “fork is copy-on-write; the cost appears only as pages are written afterwards.”

takeaways: A process owns memory, files and credentials; threads share them.
fork copies lazily (copy-on-write); exec replaces the program.
Processes isolate crashes and privileges; threads share data cheaply.
Parents must wait on children or zombies accumulate.

interactive.title: What happens to the other threads?
interactive.prompt: A web server process runs 16 worker threads. One thread dereferences an invalid pointer and the kernel sends a segmentation fault.

choices.label: The whole process, all 16 threads, is terminated
choices.feedback: Right: the default action for SIGSEGV terminates the process, and threads share it.

choices.label: Only the faulting thread stops
choices.feedback: Signals like SIGSEGV act on the process unless handled; there is no per-thread crash by default.

choices.label: The kernel restarts the faulting thread
choices.feedback: Nothing restarts threads automatically; a supervisor would restart the process.

interactive.reveal: Threads share fate. Isolation from crashes needs separate processes plus a supervisor that restarts them.

title: CPU Scheduling and Context Switching
objectives: Explain what a context switch saves and costs
Describe how a fair scheduler shares a CPU
Reason about time slices, run queues and latency

cards.title: More runnable threads than cores
cards.body: A core runs one thread at a time. The scheduler decides which runnable thread runs next and for how long, and switches between them many times a second so each makes progress. Threads waiting for I/O or a lock are not runnable and use no CPU.

cards.title: What a context switch does
cards.body: To switch, the kernel saves the running thread’s registers and program counter, picks the next thread, and restores its state. Switching to a thread in another process also switches the memory mappings, which can flush cached address translations. The direct cost is commonly a few microseconds; the indirect cost of colder caches can be larger.

cards.title: Worked example: the time-slice trade-off
cards.body: Round-robin scheduling gives each runnable thread a slice of time in turn.
steps: Assume a context switch costs 5 µs and 11 threads are runnable on one core (illustrative)
With 1 ms slices: 5 ÷ (1,000 + 5) ≈ 0.5% of the CPU goes on switching; a thread waits up to 10 × 1 = 10 ms to run again
With 10 ms slices: overhead ≈ 0.05%; waiting can reach 100 ms
Shorter slices mean responsiveness, longer slices mean throughput

cards.title: Misconception: more threads means more throughput
cards.body: Once every core is busy, extra CPU-bound threads add no capacity. They only add switching, cache misses and memory for stacks. For CPU-heavy work, a thread count close to the number of cores is usually best; extra threads help only when threads spend time waiting on I/O.

cards.title: Trap: a busy-waiting thread
cards.body: A thread that spins in a loop checking a flag stays runnable and burns its whole slice, slowing every other thread on that core. Waiting should block (on a lock, condition variable or I/O readiness) so the scheduler can run something useful.

cards.title: Edge case: the container sees every host core
cards.body: A container limited to 2 CPUs by a CFS quota may still report the host’s 64 cores. A runtime that sizes its thread pool or garbage collector from that number starts dozens of busy threads, uses up the quota early in each 100 ms period and is throttled for the rest, which shows up as latency spikes. Size pools from the cgroup limit; many modern runtimes now read it.

questions.prompt: What must the kernel save when it switches threads?

choices.label: Every open file’s contents
The process’s source code
The thread’s whole heap
Registers and the program counter

questions.explanation: Execution state lives in registers; memory stays where it is.

questions.prompt: A thread is blocked waiting for a disk read. How much CPU does it use?

choices.label: Half a slice, to keep polling
A fixed 1% reserved for it
Its full time slice each round
None until the read completes

questions.explanation: Blocked threads leave the run queue until woken.

questions.prompt: Shrinking the time slice mostly trades what for what?

choices.label: Fewer threads for more cores
Less memory for more CPU
Larger stacks for less I/O
More switching for lower latency

questions.explanation: More frequent switches cost overhead but let waiting threads run sooner.

questions.prompt: A 4-core machine runs a CPU-bound job. Which thread count is a sensible start?

choices.label: Exactly 1
About 4
One per request in flight
About 400

questions.explanation: More CPU-bound threads than cores only add switching.

questions.prompt: One core, 21 runnable CPU-bound threads, round robin with 5 ms slices. Worst-case milliseconds before a thread runs again?
assumptions: Each other thread uses its full slice
Switch cost ignored
questions.explanation: Design implication: interactive work stuck behind 20 CPU-bound threads waits about 100 ms, so latency-sensitive work needs fewer competitors or a higher priority.

questions.prompt: A request handler waits for a lock held by another thread for about 2 ms.

approaches.label: Sleep a fixed 10 ms, then try again
Spin in a loop checking the lock
Block on the lock so the thread sleeps until it is released

rationaleOptions.label: A fixed sleep wakes exactly on time
Spinning is faster for any wait
Sleeping threads give their CPU to others
The kernel wakes the thread when the lock is free

rationaleConflicts.r3: Spinning helps only for very short waits; 2 ms of spinning wastes a whole slice.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It adds up to 10 ms of extra latency after the lock is free.

questions.explanation: Block for waits longer than a context switch; spin only for waits of a few microseconds.

flashcards.back: Saving one thread’s CPU state and restoring another’s.
Lower latency, more switching overhead.
No, they leave the run queue until woken.

sources.title: Linux kernel docs: CFS scheduler design

mechanism.title: How a general-purpose scheduler shares cores
steps: Each core has a run queue of runnable threads. A thread leaves it when it blocks (I/O, lock, sleep) and rejoins when woken. Preemption happens on a timer tick or when a higher-priority thread wakes, so one thread cannot hold a core forever.

Linux’s CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) tracked each thread’s weighted run time and always ran the one that had received the least; since kernel 6.6 the default policy uses EEVDF, which also accounts for how late each thread is. Both aim to share CPU in proportion to weights set by nice values.

Real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR) sit above normal threads: a runnable real-time thread always runs before normal ones. That is useful for audio or control loops and dangerous for anything that might spin.

A context switch saves registers, switches the kernel stack and, across processes, switches page tables. The CPU’s caches and translation buffers then hold the previous thread’s data, so the new thread runs slower until they warm up.

Waking a thread on another core and moving threads between cores to balance load both cost cache warmth. Schedulers prefer to keep a thread on the core it last ran on, and you can pin threads (CPU affinity) for latency-critical work.

Measure, do not guess: per-thread run time, voluntary versus involuntary context switches (reported per process by the kernel) and run-queue length show whether threads are starved of CPU or simply waiting on I/O.

useWhen: Use a CPU-bound thread count near the core count.
Use blocking waits (locks, condition variables, readiness APIs) instead of spinning.
avoidWhen: Avoid thousands of runnable threads per core; switching and cache misses dominate.
Avoid real-time priorities for code that might loop or block on others.

rows: Pinning a thread to a core

numbers.title: How many context switches a busy server does
assumptions: A server handles 20,000 requests a second (illustrative)
Each request blocks twice (database call, then network write), causing a switch each time it blocks and each time it wakes
steps: Switches ≈ 20,000 × 2 blocks × 2 (out and back in) = 80,000 per second.
At about 5 µs each, that is 0.4 CPU-seconds per second: 40% of one core.
Spread across 8 cores, about 5% of total CPU goes to switching.
An event loop that handles many sockets per thread avoids most of these switches, which is part of why it scales to many connections.
numbers.result: Context switches are cheap one at a time but add up to a measurable share of CPU at tens of thousands of requests a second.

india.title: The Linux scheduler moved from CFS to EEVDF
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel documentation describes CFS as modelling an “ideal, precise multi-tasking CPU” by tracking virtual run time, and documents EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First), which replaced it as the default in Linux 6.6. EEVDF keeps proportional fairness but also gives each task a virtual deadline, which improves latency for tasks that run in short bursts.

pitfalls.trap: “Add more threads, the server will go faster.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if threads are waiting on I/O; for CPU-bound work beyond the core count they just add switching.”

pitfalls.trap: “Context switches are free.”
pitfalls.say: “A few microseconds each plus cache effects; at 80,000 a second that is a noticeable share of a core.”

takeaways: The scheduler shares cores among runnable threads; blocked threads use no CPU.
A context switch saves and restores CPU state and cools caches.
Short slices favour latency; long slices favour throughput.
Match CPU-bound threads to cores; block rather than spin.

interactive.title: Pick a time slice
interactive.prompt: A core has 11 runnable threads and each context switch costs 5 µs. Slide the time slice and watch overhead against how long a thread waits to run again.
interactive.takeaway: Below about 0.5 ms the CPU spends over 1% just switching; above 10 ms a thread can wait over 100 ms for its turn. Schedulers pick slices in the low milliseconds, and the real fix for long waits is fewer runnable threads.

title: Virtual Memory and Paging
objectives: Explain how virtual addresses map to physical memory
Distinguish minor and major page faults
Predict what happens when memory runs out

cards.title: Every process sees its own address space
cards.body: Programs use virtual addresses. The memory management unit translates them to physical addresses using page tables the kernel maintains, in fixed-size pages (commonly 4 KB). Two processes can use the same virtual address for different physical memory, which is how isolation works.

cards.title: Pages are loaded on demand
cards.body: The kernel does not load a program’s whole file or allocate all requested memory up front. The first touch of a page causes a page fault, and the kernel then maps a physical page. A minor fault finds the data already in memory (for example in the page cache); a major fault must read it from disk.

cards.title: Worked example: why a translation cache matters
cards.body: Each memory access needs a translation, so CPUs cache recent ones in a translation lookaside buffer (TLB).
steps: Assume 4 KB pages and a TLB with 1,536 entries (illustrative)
Memory covered without a page-table walk: 1,536 × 4 KB = 6 MB
A program touching 1 GB randomly misses the TLB often, and each miss walks several levels of page tables
With 2 MB “huge” pages, the same 1,536 entries cover 3 GB
That is why databases and JVM-style runtimes often offer huge-page settings

cards.title: Misconception: free memory is wasted memory, so the box is full
cards.body: Tools often show little “free” memory because the kernel uses spare RAM as a page cache for files. That memory is reclaimable: it is dropped when programs need it. The useful number is available memory, not free memory.

cards.title: Trap: assuming allocation means memory exists
cards.body: On Linux, allocations are usually overcommitted: asking for memory succeeds, and physical pages are assigned only when touched. If many processes then touch what they asked for, the system runs out and the out-of-memory killer terminates a process, often the largest, rather than the allocation failing cleanly.

cards.title: Edge case: adding up resident memory overcounts
cards.body: Resident set size (RSS) counts every page a process has in memory, including shared library code and shared memory that other processes map too. Summing RSS across 50 worker processes that share 200 MB of code counts that 200 MB fifty times. Proportional set size (PSS) divides each shared page among the processes using it, so it adds up correctly; use it, or the cgroup’s total, when sizing a machine. In containers the memory limit, not the sum of RSS, decides when the kill comes.

questions.prompt: Two processes print the same pointer value. Do they share that memory?

choices.label: Not necessarily; each has its own mapping
No, the kernel forbids equal addresses
Yes, a pointer value names one physical byte
Yes, if both processes run the same program

questions.explanation: Each process has its own page tables, so the same virtual address can map to different physical pages, or to the same page only if they deliberately share memory. Pointers are virtual, not physical; running the same program gives the same layout, not the same pages; and the kernel happily lets equal addresses exist in different processes.

questions.prompt: Which page fault is the expensive one?

choices.label: A major fault that reads from disk
A fault on a page already mapped
A fault on the stack guard page
A minor fault on a page already in the page cache

questions.explanation: A major fault must wait for storage to read the page, which costs microseconds to milliseconds. A minor fault on a page already in the page cache only updates the page table, a fault on an already-mapped page is a permission or copy-on-write fault handled in memory, and a guard-page fault signals stack overflow rather than costing I/O.

questions.prompt: A monitoring tool shows 200 MB free on a 16 GB server with 9 GB of page cache. Is it short of memory?

choices.label: Probably not; page cache is reclaimable
Yes, it is about to swap
Yes, the OOM killer will fire
Only if swap is turned off

questions.explanation: Look at available memory, which counts reclaimable cache.

questions.prompt: Processes touch more memory than RAM plus swap can hold. What usually happens on Linux?

choices.label: The OOM killer ends a process
Every process pauses until memory frees
The kernel compresses all code pages
The allocation call returns an error

questions.explanation: With overcommit the failure shows up at touch time, not at allocation.

questions.prompt: A TLB has 1,024 entries of 2 MB pages. How many MB of memory does it cover?
assumptions: Every entry holds a distinct 2 MB page
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same TLB with 4 KB pages covers only 4 MB, which is why huge pages help large in-memory data sets.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on the first read of a page from a memory-mapped file that is not cached.

items.label: The kernel finds the file page is not in memory
The kernel maps the page and the instruction is retried
The kernel reads the page from disk into the page cache
The CPU finds no valid translation and raises a page fault

questions.explanation: Fault, look up, read, map, retry.

flashcards.back: An access to a page with no valid mapping, handled by the kernel.
Minor: data already in memory; major: must read from disk.
A CPU cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.

mechanism.title: From a virtual address to a physical page
steps: A virtual address is split into a page number and an offset. The page number is looked up in multi-level page tables (four or five levels on 64-bit x86) to find the physical page; the offset selects the byte inside it.

The TLB caches recent translations. A TLB hit costs almost nothing; a miss triggers a page-table walk through memory. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) reduce the number of entries needed for large data sets.
Mappings carry permissions (read, write, execute) and flags such as present and dirty. Writing to a read-only shared page (as after fork) causes a fault the kernel resolves by copying the page.

Memory comes in two kinds: anonymous memory (heap, stacks) and file-backed memory (program code, memory-mapped files, the page cache). Under pressure, clean file pages can simply be dropped and re-read later; anonymous pages must go to swap if there is any.

The kernel reclaims memory in the background when free memory falls below watermarks. If reclaim cannot keep up, allocations stall in direct reclaim, which shows up as latency spikes before any process is killed.

When memory is exhausted, the out-of-memory killer picks a victim using a badness score (mostly memory use, adjustable per process). In containers, a cgroup memory limit triggers the same mechanism for processes inside that group.

useWhen: Use available memory (including reclaimable cache) to judge headroom.
Use huge pages for large, long-lived in-memory data such as database buffers.
avoidWhen: Avoid sizing a heap to almost all of RAM; the page cache and other processes need room.
Avoid treating swap activity as harmless on latency-sensitive servers.

rows: First touch, copy-on-write, cached file page

numbers.title: How major faults turn into latency
assumptions: A service handles a request with 50 page touches, normally all in memory (illustrative)
Under memory pressure, 2% of touches become major faults costing 100 µs each on SSD
steps: Faulting touches per request: 50 × 0.02 = 1.
Added time: 1 × 100 µs = 0.1 ms on average.
But faults cluster: a request that hits 10 faults waits an extra 1 ms, and on spinning disks (about 10 ms per read) 10 faults add 100 ms.
So the tail latency grows long before average latency moves.
numbers.result: Memory pressure hurts tail latency first; watch major faults, not only free memory.

india.title: Kernel documentation on memory management concepts
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s admin guide explains virtual memory, huge pages, zones, page cache, anonymous memory, reclaim and the OOM killer in one place. It notes that the kernel uses otherwise unused memory to cache file data and reclaims it under pressure, and that when reclaim fails the OOM killer selects a task to kill to free memory.

pitfalls.trap: “The server has no free memory, we need more RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “Most of it is page cache; I’d check available memory and major fault rates first.”

pitfalls.trap: “If malloc succeeded, the memory is ours.”
pitfalls.say: “With overcommit, pages are assigned on first touch; the failure can come later as an OOM kill.”

takeaways: Virtual addresses map to physical pages through page tables cached in the TLB.
Major page faults read from disk and hurt tail latency.
Page cache is reclaimable; judge headroom by available memory.
Overcommit moves out-of-memory failures to touch time and the OOM killer.

interactive.title: Which process is killed?
interactive.prompt: A container has a 1 GB memory limit. Its app grows to 1.1 GB of touched heap. The host has 64 GB free.

choices.label: A process inside the container, by the OOM killer
choices.feedback: Right: the cgroup limit applies regardless of host memory.

choices.label: Nothing: the host has plenty of memory
choices.feedback: The limit is per cgroup, so host free memory does not help.

choices.label: The allocation call fails and the app handles it
choices.feedback: With overcommit, the failure comes at touch time as a kill.

interactive.reveal: Container memory limits are enforced by the same OOM mechanism, scoped to the container’s cgroup.

title: System Calls and the Kernel Boundary
objectives: Explain why programs enter the kernel for I/O
Estimate the cost of crossing the boundary
Reduce the number of system calls on a hot path

cards.title: User mode and kernel mode
cards.body: Applications run in user mode, where the CPU blocks direct access to hardware and other processes’ memory. To open a file, send on a socket or create a process, a program makes a system call: a controlled entry into the kernel, which checks permissions and does the work.

cards.title: What a system call costs
cards.body: A system call switches privilege level, saves some state and runs kernel code. A trivial call costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds to a microsecond on modern hardware, more with some security mitigations enabled. The work inside (copying data, waiting for I/O) usually dominates.

cards.title: Worked example: buffering cuts system calls
cards.body: Writing a 1 MB log one line at a time versus in blocks.
steps: Assume 100-byte lines and 1 µs per write call (illustrative)
Unbuffered: 1,000,000 ÷ 100 = 10,000 write calls ≈ 10 ms of call overhead
Buffered in 64 KB blocks: 1,000,000 ÷ 65,536 ≈ 16 calls ≈ 16 µs
Same bytes, about 600× fewer calls
The trade-off: buffered lines may be lost if the process crashes before the buffer is flushed

cards.title: Misconception: a write call means the data is on disk
cards.body: write copies data into the kernel’s page cache and usually returns at once. The kernel writes it to storage later. Only an explicit flush such as fsync waits for the device. A machine crash can lose data that write already “accepted”.

cards.title: Trap: chatty I/O on a hot path
cards.body: Reading a file a byte at a time, or sending a response in many tiny socket writes, multiplies system calls and, for sockets, packets. Batch: read and write in larger buffers, gather several buffers in one call, or let the library buffer for you.

cards.title: Edge case: interrupted system calls
cards.body: A blocking system call such as read can return early with the error EINTR when a signal arrives. Code that treats every error as fatal then fails at random under signals used for timers or profilers. Retry on EINTR (or install handlers with SA_RESTART so the kernel restarts many calls), and handle partial reads and writes by looping until all bytes are done.

questions.prompt: Why can a program not write to the disk controller directly?

choices.label: User mode blocks hardware access
The file system locks the device for its own use
Disks only accept kernel threads
The compiler removes such code

questions.explanation: The CPU runs programs in user mode, where instructions that touch device registers fault; only the kernel, in privileged mode, drives hardware, and programs ask it through system calls. The file system is kernel code that also goes through drivers, devices do not check which kind of thread is asking, and compilers emit whatever instructions you write.

questions.prompt: A program writes 1 MB in 10-byte calls. What is the main waste?

choices.label: Each call forces the disk head to seek again
Per-call overhead on 100,000 calls
The page cache is disabled
The page cache flushes to disk after each call

questions.explanation: Each write is a system call with fixed overhead, so 1 MB in 10-byte calls makes 100,000 transitions into the kernel; buffer in user space and write in large chunks. The page cache absorbs small writes, so neither seeks nor flushes happen per call, and the page cache is not disabled by small writes.

questions.prompt: write returned success. Is the data safe from a power cut?

choices.label: Yes, if the file was opened
Yes, write waits for the disk
Only on solid-state drives
No, not until it is flushed (fsync)

questions.explanation: write lands in the page cache; durability needs an explicit flush.

questions.prompt: Which change cuts system calls when serving many small responses?

choices.label: Raising the process priority
Using smaller socket buffers
Combining buffers into one write
Adding a thread per response

questions.explanation: Gathering data into fewer calls cuts the fixed overhead.

questions.prompt: A loop makes 2 million system calls a second at 0.5 µs of overhead each. How many CPU-milliseconds of overhead per second?
assumptions: Overhead only, no work inside the calls
questions.explanation: Design implication: that is a whole core spent just crossing the boundary, so batching is worth more than tuning the work inside.

questions.prompt: Order a read from a file through the kernel.

items.label: The kernel returns the byte count and the CPU returns to user mode
The kernel copies data from the page cache (reading the disk if needed)
The program calls read with a buffer and length
The CPU switches to kernel mode

questions.explanation: Enter, work, copy, return.

flashcards.back: A controlled entry into the kernel to request a privileged service.
No; it reaches the page cache. fsync waits for the device.
Buffer and batch: fewer, larger calls.

mechanism.title: Crossing into the kernel and back
steps: The CPU has privilege levels. User code cannot execute privileged instructions or touch kernel memory; attempting to do so raises a fault. A system call uses a dedicated instruction that jumps to a fixed kernel entry point with arguments in registers.

The kernel validates every argument: file descriptors must belong to the process, pointers must point into its memory, and permissions are checked against its credentials. This is what lets many untrusting programs share one machine.

Data usually crosses the boundary by copying between user buffers and kernel buffers. Mechanisms such as memory mapping files or sending a file directly to a socket avoid some copies for large transfers.
Some frequent calls avoid the boundary entirely: on Linux the vDSO maps a small piece of kernel-provided code into every process so that reading the clock does not need a real system call.

Blocking calls such as read on an empty socket put the thread to sleep in the kernel until data arrives. Non-blocking calls return immediately with “would block”, and readiness APIs let one call wait for many descriptors.
Tracing tools count and time system calls per process, which is often the quickest way to see why a program is slow: thousands of tiny reads, repeated failed opens, or long waits in a single call.

useWhen: Use buffered I/O for many small reads and writes.
Use tracing of system calls when a program is slow and its own logs say nothing.
avoidWhen: Avoid one system call per byte or per tiny message on hot paths.
Avoid assuming a successful write survives a power cut.

rows: One slow call, but data is durable
Page faults instead of calls; errors arrive as signals

numbers.title: What a chatty logger costs at scale
assumptions: A service writes 5,000 log lines a second, one write call each, at 2 µs per call including copying (illustrative)
steps: Overhead: 5,000 × 2 µs = 10 ms of CPU each second, about 1% of a core.
If each line is also fsynced at 1 ms, the logger needs 5 seconds of device time each second: it cannot keep up and the app blocks on logging.
Buffering lines and flushing every 100 ms cuts calls to about 10 per second.
The cost is up to 100 ms of log lines lost if the machine crashes, usually acceptable for logs, not for payments.
numbers.result: Per-call overhead is small; per-call fsync is not. Batch the flush and decide how much loss is acceptable.

india.title: The kernel’s published system-call interface
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux man-pages project documents every system call, its arguments, errors and caveats. Its syscalls(2) page lists hundreds of calls, and fsync(2) states that the call transfers modified data to the storage device and blocks until the device reports completion, which is the precise difference between writing a file and making it durable.

pitfalls.trap: “We call write, so the data is saved.”
pitfalls.say: “It is in the page cache; I’d fsync where durability matters, and batch to keep the cost down.”

pitfalls.trap: “The kernel is a black box, we cannot see what the app does.”
pitfalls.say: “Tracing system calls shows every read, write and wait the process makes.”

takeaways: System calls are controlled entries into the kernel for privileged work.
Each call has fixed overhead; batch to reduce it.
write reaches the page cache; fsync makes data durable.
Trace system calls to see what a slow program is waiting on.

choices.label: The disk is slow at sequential reads

title: I/O Models: Blocking, Non-blocking and Event Loops
objectives: Compare thread-per-connection with readiness-based event loops
Explain what a readiness API reports
Spot work that blocks an event loop

cards.title: Most server time is waiting
cards.body: A request handler often spends milliseconds waiting for a database or network and microseconds computing. How a server waits decides how many connections it can hold: with one blocked thread each, or with one thread watching many sockets.

cards.title: Readiness: ask the kernel which sockets are ready
cards.body: Instead of blocking on one socket, a thread registers many sockets with a readiness API (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD) and waits once. The kernel returns the sockets that can be read or written without blocking, and the thread handles each in turn.

cards.title: Worked example: memory for 10,000 idle connections
cards.body: Compare one thread per connection with an event loop.
steps: Assume each thread reserves a 1 MB stack and touches about 64 KB of it (illustrative)
Thread per connection: 10,000 threads ≈ 640 MB actually used, 10 GB of address space reserved
Event loop: one thread plus a few KB of state per connection ≈ 10,000 × 4 KB = 40 MB
Thread switching also grows with active connections
Result: event loops suit many mostly idle connections, such as chat or streaming

cards.title: Misconception: an event loop runs things in parallel
cards.body: One event-loop thread handles one callback at a time. It is concurrent (many connections in progress) but not parallel. Using several cores needs several loops or a worker pool for CPU-heavy work.

cards.title: Trap: blocking the loop
cards.body: A callback that does a long computation, a blocking file read or a synchronous network call freezes every connection on that loop. Move CPU-heavy or blocking work to a worker pool and resume when it finishes.

cards.title: Edge case: edge-triggered readiness
cards.body: With epoll in edge-triggered mode, the kernel reports a socket once when new data arrives, not while data remains. A handler that reads one buffer and returns leaves the rest unread with no further notification, so the connection stalls. In edge-triggered mode, read until the call returns EAGAIN; level-triggered mode is simpler when unsure.

questions.prompt: A server watches 5,000 sockets with epoll. The wait call returns 3 of them. What does that tell the server?

choices.label: Three requests have been fully processed
Three sockets can be read or written now
Three threads are idle and can take work
Three sockets have used the most CPU

questions.explanation: Readiness means the next read or write on those 3 descriptors will not block: data has arrived, or there is buffer space to send. The program still does the reading, parsing and handling itself; epoll knows nothing about threads, request completion or CPU use.

questions.prompt: One callback on an event loop parses a 200 MB file synchronously. What do other clients see?

choices.label: Faster replies from cached data
The kernel resets their connections at once
Their requests stall until it finishes
Nothing; the loop runs them in parallel

questions.explanation: An event loop runs one callback at a time on its thread, so every other client waits until the parse finishes. The kernel keeps accepting and queuing connections rather than resetting them, nothing runs in parallel on a single loop, and no cache makes replies faster. Move the parse to a worker or stream it in chunks.

questions.prompt: Which workload best suits an event loop over thread per connection?

choices.label: One connection doing heavy maths
Short scripts run once a day
Many idle long-lived connections
A few CPU-heavy batch jobs

questions.explanation: Many idle long-lived connections, such as chat or live cricket scores, need only a few KB of state each on a loop, against a thread stack each. Heavy maths and CPU-bound batch jobs gain nothing from an event loop, and a daily script has no connections to multiplex.

questions.prompt: An event-loop server pins one core at 100% while others idle. A fitting fix?

choices.label: Add a thread per connection
Lower the loop’s priority
Run one loop per core
Make every socket blocking

questions.explanation: One loop runs on one thread, so it uses one core; run one loop per core, often as several processes sharing the port, to use them all. A thread per connection abandons the event model, lowering priority only makes it slower, and blocking sockets would stall the loop.

questions.prompt: Order one turn of a server’s readiness-based loop.

items.label: Queue responses and write what the sockets accept
Read available bytes from each ready socket
Wait on the readiness API for ready sockets
Run the handlers for complete requests

questions.explanation: Wait, read, handle, write, repeat.

questions.prompt: A notification service holds 200,000 mostly idle connections and sends small messages.
constraints: Messages are small and cheap to build

approaches.label: An event loop per core using a readiness API

rationaleOptions.label: Threads are always simpler to scale
Idle connections cost only a little state
No thread stack or switch per idle client
Event loops make CPU work free

rationaleConflicts.r3: 200,000 stacks and the switching between them cost far more memory and CPU.
rationaleConflicts.r4: CPU work still costs the same and blocks the loop if done inline.

questions.explanation: Pick the I/O model by how connections spend their time: mostly waiting favours event loops.

flashcards.back: Blocking waits in the call; non-blocking returns “would block” at once.
Waits on many descriptors and reports the ready ones.
Never block or compute for long in a callback.

mechanism.title: How the kernel lets one thread wait on many sockets
steps: Blocking I/O: read on a socket with no data puts the thread to sleep until data arrives. Simple to write, but each waiting connection holds a thread.
Non-blocking I/O: with O_NONBLOCK set, read returns immediately with EAGAIN when no data is available. On its own this would force polling, so it is paired with a readiness API.

epoll keeps an interest list of descriptors inside the kernel. epoll_wait returns only the ready ones, so the cost per wait depends on how many are ready, not how many are registered, unlike the older select and poll calls that scan every descriptor.

Edge-triggered mode reports a descriptor only when it becomes ready; the program must then read until EAGAIN or it may never be told again. Level-triggered mode keeps reporting while data remains, which is more forgiving.

Regular files do not fit the readiness model: select and poll always report them ready and epoll refuses to register them, even though a read may wait for the disk. Event-loop runtimes therefore send file I/O and other blocking calls to a thread pool. Completion-based interfaces (such as io_uring on Linux) let the kernel finish the operation and report completion instead.
Production servers usually combine models: one event loop per core for network I/O, plus a bounded worker pool for CPU-heavy or blocking work, with back-pressure when the pool’s queue fills.

useWhen: Use event loops for many concurrent, mostly idle connections.
Use a worker pool alongside the loop for CPU-heavy or blocking calls.
avoidWhen: Avoid long computations or blocking calls inside loop callbacks.
Avoid edge-triggered mode unless the code always drains reads until EAGAIN.

rows: Memory and switching at high connection counts

numbers.title: How long a blocking callback stalls a loop
assumptions: One loop serves 5,000 active connections, each sending a request every second (illustrative)
A handler occasionally does a 50 ms synchronous computation
steps: The loop handles about 5,000 requests a second, about 0.2 ms each on average.
During a 50 ms stall about 250 requests arrive and wait.
Those 250 requests each gain up to 50 ms of latency, which shows in p99 even if stalls are rare.
Moving the computation to a worker pool keeps the loop’s turn time near 0.2 ms.
numbers.result: One slow callback adds its full duration to every request waiting behind it.

india.title: Readiness notification documented by the kernel
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The epoll(7) manual describes the interest and ready lists, the difference between edge- and level-triggered modes, and gives an example loop. It warns that with edge-triggered mode a program should use non-blocking descriptors and wait only after a read or write returns EAGAIN, a rule many hand-written event loops have broken by accident.

pitfalls.trap: “Our event-loop server is single-threaded, so it cannot use 8 cores.”
pitfalls.say: “Run one loop per core, or several processes, and spread connections across them.”

pitfalls.trap: “The disk read is async because the file descriptor is non-blocking.”
pitfalls.say: “Regular files ignore non-blocking mode; that read can block the loop, so it belongs in a worker pool.”

takeaways: Thread per connection is simple; event loops scale to many idle connections.
Readiness APIs report which descriptors can proceed without blocking.
Never block or compute for long inside a loop callback.
Combine loops with a worker pool and back-pressure.

interactive.prompt: An event-loop server has 3,000 open connections. One request triggers a 2-second synchronous image resize inside its callback.

choices.label: All 3,000 connections pause for about 2 seconds
choices.feedback: Right: the loop thread is busy and cannot service any other socket.

choices.label: Only the requesting connection waits
choices.feedback: That would be true with thread per connection, not a single loop.

choices.label: The kernel moves the work to another core
choices.feedback: The kernel schedules threads, not callbacks; nothing splits the work.

interactive.reveal: CPU-heavy work belongs in a worker pool so the loop keeps serving other connections.

title: Race Conditions and Mutual Exclusion
objectives: Recognise a data race in read-modify-write code
Use a mutex to protect a critical section
Keep critical sections short and consistent

cards.title: Two threads, one counter
cards.body: count = count + 1 is three steps: read, add, write. If two threads read the same value before either writes, one increment is lost. The result depends on timing, so the bug appears rarely in tests and often under load.

cards.title: A mutex makes a section exclusive
cards.body: A mutex (mutual-exclusion lock) lets only one thread at a time run a critical section. Threads that try to lock it while it is held wait. Every access to the shared data must go through the same lock, or the protection is incomplete.

cards.title: Worked example: how many increments are lost
cards.body: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter 1,000,000 times without a lock.
steps: Expected total: 2,000,000
Each lost update happens when both threads read the same value
Runs on a multi-core machine commonly print totals well below 2,000,000, and a different total each time
With a mutex around the increment, or an atomic add instruction, the total is exactly 2,000,000
The atomic version is faster here because the critical section is a single instruction

cards.title: Misconception: it only reads, so it needs no lock
cards.body: Reading while another thread writes can see a half-updated structure: a list whose pointer is updated but whose length is not, or a 64-bit value torn into two halves on some platforms. Readers of data that others write need the same lock, a read-write lock, or an atomic type.

cards.title: Trap: holding a lock during slow work
cards.body: A lock held across a network call or a disk write makes every other thread that needs it wait for that I/O. Copy what you need under the lock, release it, then do the slow work.

cards.title: Failure story: a race in a radiation machine
cards.body: Documented by Leveson and Turner (IEEE Computer, 1993): between 1985 and 1987 the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine gave massive overdoses in six known accidents. One cause was a race between the operator’s fast edits and the task setting up the beam, so the machine could fire in a state the screen did not show, and hardware interlocks from earlier models had been removed. Races that tests rarely hit can still be fatal.

questions.prompt: Why does count = count + 1 lose updates across threads?

choices.label: It is a read, an add and a write
Integers are not stored in memory
Threads have separate copies of globals
The compiler skips repeated additions

questions.explanation: Two threads can both read 5, both add 1 and both write 6, so one increment vanishes. The counter is ordinary shared memory, and threads share globals, which is the whole problem; nothing is skipping additions, the interleaving loses them.

questions.prompt: One code path updates a shared map under lock L; another reads it with no lock. Is the data protected?

choices.label: Yes, writers hold the lock
Yes, reads are always atomic
Only on single-core machines
No, every access must use L

questions.explanation: A lock protects data only if all accesses agree to use it.

questions.prompt: A thread holds a lock while calling a payment API that takes 300 ms. What happens to others?

choices.label: They run the call in parallel
The lock times out after 1 ms
They wait up to 300 ms for the lock
Nothing; locks pause during I/O

questions.explanation: The lock is held for the whole call, so every thread that needs it queues for up to 300 ms, and the lock allows only about 3 such calls a second. Locks do not time out or pause during I/O by themselves. Copy what you need under the lock, release it, then call the API.

questions.prompt: A checkout race shows up once in a million test runs. During a sale, production handles 5 million checkouts a day. What should you expect?

choices.label: It will not appear, as tests are harsher
Several failures a day, likely more at peak
5 failures, one per million, every day
No failures, as production servers are faster

questions.explanation: At one in a million, 5 million checkouts is already about 5 a day, and real concurrency at peak usually makes the bad interleaving more likely, not less. A probability gives an expected count, not a fixed one, and faster or busier machines change the timing in ways that often expose races.

questions.prompt: Order the interleaving that loses an update (counter starts at 5).

items.label: Thread B reads 5
Thread A reads 5
Thread A writes 6
Thread B writes 6

questions.explanation: Both computed from the same old value.

questions.prompt: Many threads increment per-endpoint request counters on every request.
constraints: Totals are read once a second

approaches.label: Use atomic add operations on each counter
One global mutex around all counters
No synchronisation; small errors are fine

rationaleOptions.label: A global mutex is always the safest choice
Unsynchronised counters are only slightly off
No thread waits behind another for an unrelated counter
A single atomic instruction needs no lock

rationaleConflicts.r3: It is correct but serialises every request on one lock.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Lost updates grow with contention and can be large.

questions.explanation: For single-variable updates use atomics; for multi-field invariants use a lock.

flashcards.back: A result that depends on the timing of concurrent operations.
Only one thread at a time runs the protected section.
Protect every access; keep slow work outside.

mechanism.title: How locks and atomics prevent races
steps: A data race is two threads accessing the same memory at the same time, at least one writing, without synchronisation. Many language memory models make the whole program’s behaviour undefined when it happens, not merely the value of one variable.

CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations for speed. Locks and atomic operations include the barriers that stop reordering across them, so data written before an unlock is visible to the next thread that locks.
An uncontended mutex lock is cheap: on Linux it is an atomic instruction in user space, and only contended locks enter the kernel through futex calls to sleep and wake waiters.

Atomic operations (add, compare-and-swap) update a single word indivisibly. They fit counters and flags; protecting an invariant across several fields still needs a lock or a carefully designed lock-free structure.
Read-write locks let many readers in at once but writers alone. They help only when reads are long and frequent; for short sections a plain mutex is often faster.
Contention, not the lock itself, is the cost: when many threads want one lock they queue and the program runs serially. Splitting data (per-core counters, sharded maps) reduces contention.

useWhen: Use a mutex for invariants across several fields.
Use atomics for independent counters and flags.
avoidWhen: Avoid reading shared mutable data without the lock or an atomic type.
Avoid holding locks across I/O or calls into unknown code.

rows: Writer starvation, overhead on short sections

numbers.title: What contention does to a hot lock
assumptions: 8 threads, each request holds a shared lock for 20 µs (illustrative)
Work outside the lock is 180 µs per request
steps: The lock can serve at most 1,000,000 ÷ 20 = 50,000 requests a second, whatever the thread count.
Without contention, 8 threads at 200 µs per request could do 8 × 5,000 = 40,000 a second, close to the lock limit.
With 16 threads the demand would be 80,000 a second, but the lock caps throughput at 50,000.
Shrinking the section to 5 µs raises the cap to 200,000 a second.
numbers.result: A lock turns its critical section into a serial bottleneck; throughput is capped at 1 ÷ hold time.

india.title: Futexes: why uncontended locks stay in user space
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The futex(2) manual explains that a futex is a 32-bit value in user memory plus a kernel wait queue. Lock and unlock are done with atomic instructions in user space, and the kernel is involved only when a thread must sleep because the lock is held, or must be woken. That design is why modern mutexes are cheap until they are contended.

pitfalls.trap: “It works on my machine, so there is no race.”
pitfalls.say: “Races depend on timing; I’d check every shared access is synchronised rather than trust tests.”

pitfalls.trap: “Reads don’t need the lock.”
pitfalls.say: “They do if anyone writes concurrently; otherwise readers can see torn or half-updated data.”

takeaways: Read-modify-write on shared data races without synchronisation.
A mutex protects data only if every access uses it.
Atomics suit single words; locks suit multi-field invariants.
Throughput through a lock is capped at 1 ÷ hold time.

interactive.title: What does it print?
interactive.prompt: Two threads each run 1,000,000 unsynchronised increments of a shared counter on a 4-core machine, then the program prints the counter.

choices.label: Usually less than 2,000,000, varying between runs
choices.feedback: Right: lost updates depend on how the threads interleave.

choices.label: Exactly 2,000,000 every time
choices.feedback: That needs a lock or an atomic add.

choices.label: Exactly 1,000,000 every time
choices.feedback: Losses are not that regular; they depend on timing.

interactive.reveal: Make the increment atomic or wrap it in a mutex and the total becomes exactly 2,000,000.
