title: Deadlocks and How to Avoid Them
objectives: Name the four conditions for deadlock
Prevent deadlock with a global lock order
Tell deadlock from livelock and starvation

cards.title: Each waits for the other
cards.body: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither can proceed, and nothing will change: a deadlock. The program does not crash, it just stops making progress on those threads.

cards.title: Four conditions, all required
cards.body: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait (holding one resource while asking for another), no preemption (resources cannot be taken away), and a circular wait. Break any one and deadlock cannot occur.

cards.title: Worked example: transfers between two accounts
cards.body: Transfer(a, b) locks a then b. Two transfers run in opposite directions.
steps: Thread 1: transfer(X, Y) locks X
Thread 2: transfer(Y, X) locks Y
Thread 1 waits for Y; thread 2 waits for X: circular wait
Fix: always lock the account with the smaller id first, whatever the direction
Both threads now try X first; one waits, the other finishes, and the cycle cannot form

cards.title: Misconception: timeouts fix deadlocks
cards.body: Giving up after a timeout turns a hang into an error, which is better than hanging forever, but under load both threads may time out, retry together and collide again (livelock). Timeouts are a safety net; a consistent lock order is the fix.

cards.title: Trap: calling unknown code while holding a lock
cards.body: A callback, a logging hook or a plugin called under your lock may take other locks in an order you cannot see. Release your locks before calling out, or document and enforce which locks callers may hold.

cards.title: Failure story: priority inversion on Mars
cards.body: Publicly reported by the Mars Pathfinder team in 1997: a low-priority task held a mutex needed by a high-priority bus task, while medium-priority tasks kept the low one from running. The high-priority task missed its deadline, and a watchdog reset the lander repeatedly. Engineers enabled priority inheritance on that mutex from Earth, so the holder temporarily ran at the waiting task’s priority.

questions.prompt: A team fixes a deadlock by making every code path take the orders lock before the payments lock. Which of the four conditions did they remove?

choices.label: Hold-and-wait
Circular wait
Mutual exclusion
No preemption

questions.explanation: Threads still hold one lock while waiting for another, the locks are still exclusive and nothing takes them away. What changed is that no thread can hold payments while waiting for orders, so a cycle cannot form. Removing hold-and-wait would mean taking both locks at once or neither.

questions.prompt: At peak, an order service stops completing orders. The process is up, its health check still answers, CPU is at 2% and the order threads are all parked waiting for locks. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: A deadlock between lock holders
A livelock of threads retrying
A busy loop on one core
Memory used up by a leak

questions.explanation: Deadlocked threads sleep, so CPU drops while the process stays up and unrelated threads such as the health check still answer. A livelock and a busy loop burn CPU, and a leak shows growing memory and out-of-memory kills, not threads parked on locks. A thread dump showing each thread waiting on a lock another holds confirms it.

questions.prompt: Two threads keep backing off and retrying in step, never progressing, CPU busy. What is this?

choices.label: Deadlock
Priority inversion
A memory leak
Livelock

questions.explanation: Livelock: the threads are active and burning CPU, but each backs off and retries in step with the other, so none progresses. A deadlock shows sleeping threads, priority inversion needs threads of different priorities, and a memory leak grows memory. Random jitter in the back-off breaks the lockstep.

questions.prompt: transfer(a, b) must lock both accounts. Which rule prevents deadlock?

choices.label: Lock the lower account id first
Lock the source account first
Lock whichever is less busy
Lock the destination first

questions.explanation: Ordering by direction (source first, or destination first) means transfer(X, Y) and transfer(Y, X) take the locks in opposite orders, so a cycle can form. A fixed global order such as the lower id first gives every pair one order. “Less busy” changes from moment to moment, so it is no order at all.

questions.prompt: Order the events in a two-lock deadlock.

items.label: Thread A locks L1
Thread B requests L1 and waits
Thread A requests L2 and waits
Thread B locks L2

questions.explanation: Each holds one lock and waits for the other.

questions.prompt: An inventory service must update stock rows for every item in an order, several at once, concurrently with other orders.

approaches.label: Sort item ids and lock them in that order
Lock items in the order they appear in the cart
One global lock for all stock

rationaleOptions.label: A global lock is the only safe choice
Every order takes locks in the same global order
Orders on different items still run in parallel
Cart order is fine because carts are small

rationaleConflicts.r3: Two carts with the same items in different order can deadlock.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It avoids deadlock but serialises unrelated orders.

questions.explanation: A consistent order across all code paths prevents cycles without serialising everything.

flashcards.back: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Acquire locks in one global order.
Threads stay busy reacting to each other but make no progress.

sources.title: Linux kernel docs: lockdep, the lock validator

mechanism.title: Preventing, detecting and recovering from deadlock
steps: Prevention removes one of the four conditions. Ordering locks removes circular wait; acquiring all locks at once (or none) removes hold-and-wait; try-lock with release removes no-preemption in practice.

Lock ordering needs a rule every code path follows: by address, by id, or by a documented hierarchy (for example, always the account lock before the ledger lock). Tools can check it: the Linux kernel’s lockdep records the order in which lock classes are taken and reports any path that could close a cycle.

Detection is how databases cope, because transactions take locks in an order the database cannot control. PostgreSQL checks for a cycle after a lock wait exceeds deadlock_timeout (1 second by default) and aborts one transaction, which the application must retry.
Livelock is the active cousin of deadlock: threads keep responding to each other without progress, for example both releasing and retrying in step. Randomised backoff breaks the symmetry.

Starvation is when one thread never gets a resource others keep taking. Priority inversion is a variant: a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, while medium-priority threads keep the low one from running; priority inheritance fixes it.
Diagnosing a hang: take a thread dump or attach a debugger and list what each thread holds and waits for. A cycle in that graph is a deadlock; a long chain to one busy holder is contention.

useWhen: Use one documented lock order across the codebase.
Use try-lock with backoff when a fixed order is impossible.
avoidWhen: Avoid calling callbacks or external code while holding locks.
Avoid relying on timeouts alone; they turn hangs into retry storms.

rows: Must know every lock in advance

numbers.title: How often opposite-order locking collides
assumptions: Two code paths take locks A and B in opposite orders (illustrative)
Each path runs 1,000 times a second and holds its first lock for 10 µs before taking the second
steps: A collision needs path 2 to grab its first lock inside path 1’s 10 µs window.
Fraction of time path 1 sits in that window: 1,000 × 10 µs = 1%.
Path 2 starts 1,000 times a second, so about 1,000 × 1% = 10 risky overlaps a second, a meaningful share of which deadlock.
In testing with 10 runs a second, the same bug might take minutes or never appear.
numbers.result: Deadlocks that are rare in tests can be near-certain at production rates; prevent them by design.

india.title: Deadlock detection in PostgreSQL
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: PostgreSQL’s documentation on explicit locking explains that it detects deadlock situations automatically and resolves them by aborting one of the transactions involved, and recommends acquiring locks on multiple objects in a consistent order in every application to avoid deadlocks in the first place. The aborted transaction gets an error and should be retried.

pitfalls.trap: “We added a timeout, so deadlocks are handled.”
pitfalls.say: “That limits the damage; I’d fix the lock order so the cycle cannot form.”

pitfalls.trap: “The service hung but CPU was idle, so it was not our code.”
pitfalls.say: “Idle CPU and stuck threads is the signature of a deadlock; a thread dump will show the cycle.”

takeaways: Deadlock needs all four conditions; break one to prevent it.
A global lock order removes circular wait.
Databases detect deadlocks and abort a transaction; retry it.
Livelock and starvation are progress failures without a full stop.

interactive.title: Will these two transfers deadlock?
interactive.prompt: Transfers always lock the lower account id first. Thread 1 runs transfer(7 → 3); thread 2 runs transfer(3 → 7) at the same moment.

choices.label: No: both try to lock account 3 first
choices.feedback: Right: the same order in both threads means one simply waits.

choices.label: Yes: they run in opposite directions
choices.feedback: Direction no longer matters once locks follow id order.

choices.label: Only if the amounts are equal
choices.feedback: Amounts have nothing to do with lock order.

interactive.reveal: Ordering by a stable key turns a potential cycle into a simple queue on the first lock.

title: Condition Variables, Semaphores and Bounded Queues
objectives: Wait for a condition without busy-waiting
Use a semaphore to limit concurrency
Build a bounded producer-consumer queue

cards.title: Waiting for something to become true
cards.body: A worker should sleep until a queue has items, not spin checking it. A condition variable lets a thread release a mutex and sleep atomically, then wake when another thread signals that the condition may have changed.

cards.title: Semaphores count permits
cards.body: A counting semaphore holds a number of permits. Acquiring takes one, waiting if none are left; releasing returns one. With 10 permits, at most 10 threads use a resource at once: a natural limit for database connections or outbound calls.

cards.title: Worked example: a bounded queue between producers and consumers
cards.body: A queue with capacity 100 sits between request handlers and workers.
steps: Producer: lock; while the queue is full, wait on “not full”; add the item; signal “not empty”; unlock
Consumer: lock; while the queue is empty, wait on “not empty”; take an item; signal “not full”; unlock
When producers outpace consumers, the queue fills and producers block: back-pressure
The capacity bounds memory, unlike an unbounded queue that grows until the process runs out

cards.title: Misconception: a wake-up means the condition is true
cards.body: Condition variables can wake spuriously, and another thread may grab the item between the signal and your wake-up. Always re-check the condition in a while loop after waking, never with a single if.

cards.title: Trap: an unbounded queue hides overload
cards.body: An unbounded in-memory queue accepts work faster than it can be done, so latency and memory grow until the process falls over. Bound the queue and decide what happens when full: block, reject, or shed the oldest work.

cards.title: Edge case: the lost wake-up
cards.body: A producer that adds an item and signals without holding the mutex can slip between a consumer’s check (queue empty) and its wait, so the signal arrives before anyone is waiting and the consumer sleeps with an item ready. Change the shared state while holding the mutex the waiters use, then signal. Use broadcast when threads wait for different conditions on one condition variable, because signal may wake a thread that cannot proceed.

questions.prompt: Why must a condition variable wait sit inside a while loop?

choices.label: Wake-ups can be spurious or stale
The loop retakes the mutex after every wake-up
It lets the wait run without holding the mutex
Each signal wakes every thread that is waiting

questions.explanation: A wait can return without a signal, and another thread may take the item between the signal and this thread running, so the condition must be re-checked after every wake-up. The wait itself retakes the mutex before returning, so the loop does not need to; the mutex must be held when the wait is called, loop or not; and signal wakes at most one waiter (broadcast wakes all).

questions.prompt: At most 20 threads may call a partner API at once. Which tool fits?

choices.label: A semaphore with 20 permits
A single mutex
A condition variable alone
A read-write lock

questions.explanation: Permits count concurrent users directly.

questions.prompt: Producers outpace consumers on a bounded queue. What happens?

choices.label: Old items are silently reordered
Consumers speed up automatically
Producers block or are rejected
Memory grows until the OOM kill

questions.explanation: That is the point of bounding: overload becomes visible back-pressure.

questions.prompt: What does waiting on a condition variable do with the mutex?

choices.label: Releases it while asleep, retakes it on wake
Keeps holding it, so signallers wait for the sleeper
Passes it to the signalling thread
Releases it for good; the waiter locks it again later

questions.explanation: Waiting atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, so a producer can lock it and change the state, and the wait retakes it before returning. Holding it while asleep would deadlock the signaller, the mutex is never handed directly to another thread, and the caller does not have to relock it after the wait returns.

questions.prompt: Order a consumer taking one item from a bounded queue.

items.label: While the queue is empty, wait on “not empty”
Lock the queue mutex
Remove one item
Signal “not full” and unlock

questions.explanation: Lock, wait in a loop, take, signal.

questions.prompt: An API enqueues image jobs for 8 workers. Traffic bursts reach 10× the processing rate for a few minutes.

approaches.label: A bounded queue that rejects with 503 and Retry-After when full
Start a new thread per job

rationaleOptions.label: Memory stays bounded during bursts
Clients learn to slow down instead of timing out
Unbounded queues never lose jobs
Thread per job adds capacity

rationaleConflicts.r3: They lose all of them when the process runs out of memory.
rationaleConflicts.r4: The 8 workers’ CPU limit is unchanged; extra threads add contention.

questions.explanation: Bound every queue and choose the overload behaviour deliberately.

flashcards.front: What is a condition variable for?
flashcards.back: Sleeping until another thread signals a change, with a mutex.
A counter of permits that limits concurrent users.
To turn overload into back-pressure instead of memory growth.

mechanism.title: Coordinating threads without spinning
steps: A condition variable is always used with a mutex and a predicate (“queue not empty”). The waiter locks, checks the predicate in a loop, and calls wait, which atomically releases the mutex and sleeps so that a signal sent after the check cannot be missed.

Signalling wakes one waiter; broadcasting wakes all. Signal is enough when any one waiter can make progress; broadcast is needed when waiters wait for different predicates on the same condition variable.
POSIX states that spurious wake-ups may occur, so the predicate must be re-checked after every wait returns. Even without spurious wake-ups, another thread may have consumed the item first.

A counting semaphore is a counter with blocking acquire and release. It needs no ownership: one thread can acquire and another release, which makes it suitable for signalling between threads and for limiting concurrency.

Bounded queues combine both ideas: two conditions (“not full”, “not empty”) or two semaphores (free slots, filled slots) plus a mutex. They are the in-process version of the message queues used between services.

Little’s law sizes them: items in the system = arrival rate × time in system. A queue that keeps growing means arrivals exceed service rate, and no capacity setting will fix it; only more workers or less work will.

useWhen: Use condition variables for “wait until state changes” inside one process.
Use semaphores to cap concurrent access to a limited resource.
avoidWhen: Avoid sleeping in a loop with a fixed delay to poll for work.
Avoid unbounded queues between stages that can run at different speeds.

rows: Forgetting to lock on some path
No policy for when it is full

numbers.title: How big should the queue be?
assumptions: Workers process 400 jobs a second in total; each job takes 20 ms to run (illustrative)
Bursts arrive at 1,000 jobs a second for up to 5 seconds; the target is under 2 seconds of queueing
steps: During a burst the backlog grows by 1,000 − 400 = 600 jobs a second.
After 5 seconds: 3,000 queued jobs, which take 3,000 ÷ 400 = 7.5 s to drain, far over the 2 s target.
A capacity of 2 s × 400 = 800 jobs keeps waits under 2 s; jobs beyond that are rejected and retried later.
A larger queue would only convert rejections into timeouts.
numbers.result: Size a queue by the waiting time you can accept, not by how much memory you have.

india.title: POSIX on spurious wake-ups
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The POSIX specification of pthread_cond_wait says that spurious wakeups may occur and that because the return from wait does not imply anything about the predicate, it should be re-evaluated on return. It also specifies that the mutex is released atomically with blocking, which is the property that prevents a lost wake-up between checking and sleeping.

pitfalls.trap: “The worker sleeps 10 ms between checks, that is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “It adds up to 10 ms latency and wastes wake-ups; a condition variable wakes it exactly when work arrives.”

pitfalls.trap: “Make the queue bigger so we never reject.”
pitfalls.say: “A bigger queue just turns rejections into timeouts; I’d size it to the wait we can accept.”

takeaways: Condition variables sleep until signalled; always re-check in a while loop.
Semaphores cap how many threads use a resource.
Bounded queues turn overload into back-pressure.
Size queues by acceptable waiting time (Little’s law).

interactive.title: Fill the worker pool
interactive.prompt: Requests arrive at 200 a second and a pool of 8 worker threads serves them. Slide how long each request holds a worker.
interactive.takeaway: At 20 ms only 4 workers are busy on average. Past 40 ms every worker is busy and the queue starts growing without limit, which is when a bounded queue and rejection keep latency predictable.

title: Files, the Page Cache and fsync
objectives: Explain how reads and writes use the page cache
Make a file write durable, including its directory entry
Write files atomically with rename

cards.title: Files go through memory
cards.body: Reads and writes normally go through the page cache: reads are served from memory when cached, and writes update cached pages that the kernel writes to storage later. That makes repeated reads fast and writes cheap, at the cost of durability until the data is flushed.

cards.title: fsync is the durability point
cards.body: fsync on a file descriptor waits until the file’s data and metadata are on stable storage. Creating or renaming a file also changes the directory, so making a new file survive a crash means syncing the directory too.

cards.title: Worked example: replacing a config file safely
cards.body: Overwriting a file in place can leave it half-written after a crash.
steps: Write the new contents to config.tmp in the same directory
fsync config.tmp so its data is on disk
rename config.tmp to config: on POSIX file systems this replaces the name atomically
fsync the directory so the rename itself is durable
After a crash, readers see either the old file or the new one, never a mix

cards.title: Misconception: closing the file flushes it to disk
cards.body: close releases the descriptor; it does not wait for the data to reach storage. Data written and closed can still be lost in a power cut until the kernel writes it back or someone calls fsync.

cards.title: Trap: ignoring fsync errors
cards.body: If fsync reports an I/O error, the kernel may already have dropped the dirty pages, so calling fsync again can return success without the data ever being written. After a failed fsync, treat the data as lost and recover from a known-good copy, as PostgreSQL now does by crashing and replaying its log.

cards.title: Edge case: fdatasync, metadata and drive caches
cards.body: fsync flushes a file’s data and all of its metadata, including size and timestamps; fdatasync skips metadata that is not needed to read the data back, such as the modification time, but still flushes a change in size, which saves a write per call for logs that overwrite space allocated in advance. On Linux either call normally also asks the device to empty its volatile write cache. A drive or virtual disk that acknowledges flushes without honouring them silently breaks durability, so test with real power loss rather than trusting the acknowledgement.

questions.prompt: A 2 GB file is read twice in a row on a server with 16 GB free. Why is the second read faster?

choices.label: It is served from the page cache
The disk remembers recent reads
The second read skips checksums
The file was compressed first

questions.explanation: The kernel keeps the 2 GB of pages in memory after the first read, and with 16 GB free nothing evicts them. A drive’s own cache is tiny by comparison, and checksums and compression do not depend on whether the file was read before.

questions.prompt: A payments ledger appends each transaction to a file, then replies “success”. Power fails a second later. Which call, made before replying, makes sure the entry survives?

choices.label: Calling close on the file
write returning the byte count
Opening the file in append mode
Calling fsync on the file

questions.explanation: write returns once the bytes are in the page cache, and close only releases the descriptor; neither waits for the device. Append mode controls where bytes go, not when they reach storage. fsync waits until the data and metadata are on stable storage, so only then is it safe to reply.

questions.prompt: A service updates settings.json in place by truncating it and writing 40 KB. A crash mid-write leaves an empty file and the service will not start. What makes the update crash-safe?

choices.label: Write the file in smaller 4 KB pieces
Write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over
Call close straight after the last write
Keep a copy of the settings in memory

questions.explanation: rename atomically switches the name to a fully written, synced file, so after a crash readers see the old settings or the new ones, never a truncated mix; fsync the directory too so the rename itself survives. Smaller writes still leave a half-written file, close does not flush to storage, and a copy in memory is gone after the crash.

questions.prompt: fsync returns an I/O error. What is the safe assumption?

choices.label: Only metadata was affected
The data is safe in the cache
The written data may be lost
Retrying fsync will save it

questions.explanation: Linux may already have dropped the dirty pages and cleared the error, so a second fsync can succeed with nothing written. Assume the data is lost and recover from a known-good copy or a log, as PostgreSQL does by crashing and replaying its write-ahead log. The failure can hit data, not just metadata, and the cache is no longer a safe copy.

questions.prompt: Order a crash-safe replacement of a file.

items.label: rename it over the original
Write the new contents to a temporary file
fsync the temporary file
fsync the containing directory

questions.explanation: Data durable, then switch the name, then make the switch durable.

questions.prompt: A disk completes about 500 fsyncs a second. A service fsyncs after each of its 2,000 writes a second. What fraction of the writes can it keep up with, in percent?
assumptions: One fsync per write
No batching
questions.explanation: Design implication: per-write fsync caps throughput at the device’s flush rate, which is why databases batch commits into group commits.

flashcards.front: What does the page cache do?
flashcards.back: Keeps file data in memory for fast reads and deferred writes.

flashcards.front: How to make a new file durable?
flashcards.back: fsync the file, then fsync its directory.
Write temp, fsync, rename over, fsync directory.

sources.title: Linux kernel docs: Memory management concepts (page cache)
PostgreSQL: Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log

mechanism.title: From write to stable storage
steps: write copies data into page-cache pages and marks them dirty. Background writeback flushes dirty pages after a delay or when too much memory is dirty, so a crash can lose the last several seconds of writes that were never synced.

fsync flushes the file’s dirty data and the metadata needed to read it back, and asks the device to flush its own write cache. fdatasync skips metadata not needed for reading, such as the modification time, and can be cheaper.

A new file’s name lives in its directory. fsync on the file does not necessarily persist that name, so durable file creation and rename also need an fsync on the directory, as the fsync(2) manual notes.

rename within one file system atomically replaces the destination name, which gives the write-temp-then-rename pattern. It does not by itself guarantee the new contents are durable, which is why the temp file is synced first.
O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache for applications such as databases that manage their own cache; O_SYNC makes each write behave as if followed by a sync. Both trade throughput for control.

Errors are reported once: if writeback fails, the error is returned to the next fsync and the pages may be marked clean. Programs that ignore fsync errors, or retry and trust the second result, can silently lose data.

useWhen: Use temp-file-plus-rename for files that must never be half-written.
Use batched fsyncs (group commit) when many writes need durability.
avoidWhen: Avoid assuming close or a successful write means durable.
Avoid retrying fsync after an error and trusting the result.

numbers.title: Why group commit matters
assumptions: A disk with a 2 ms flush latency (illustrative)
10,000 small transactions a second, each needing durability
steps: One fsync per transaction: at most 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 flushes a second, far below 10,000.
Group commit: gather all transactions that arrive during a flush and sync them together.
With a flush every 2 ms, each flush carries about 20 transactions, so 10,000 a second fit in 500 flushes.
Each transaction waits at most about one flush interval longer.
numbers.result: Batching durability turns a device-bound limit into a latency cost of about one flush.

india.title: The fsync error-handling change in PostgreSQL
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: In 2018 PostgreSQL developers publicly discussed that, on Linux, a failed fsync could clear the error and drop the dirty pages, so a later successful fsync did not mean the data was written. PostgreSQL changed its behaviour to treat an fsync failure as fatal (PANIC) and recover from the write-ahead log, as its reliability documentation now describes for data_sync_retry.

pitfalls.trap: “We close the file, so it is saved.”
pitfalls.say: “close does not flush; I’d fsync the file and, for new names, the directory.”

pitfalls.trap: “fsync failed, so we just call it again.”
pitfalls.say: “The kernel may have dropped those pages; a second success proves nothing. Treat it as data loss and recover.”

takeaways: Writes land in the page cache; fsync makes them durable.
New names need the directory synced too.
Write temp, fsync, rename, fsync directory for atomic replacement.
Treat fsync errors as data loss; batch fsyncs for throughput.

interactive.title: What survives the power cut?
interactive.prompt: An app writes 10 MB to a new file, calls close, and prints “saved”. Two seconds later the power fails.

choices.label: Possibly nothing: the data may still be only in the page cache
choices.feedback: Right: neither close nor write waits for storage.

choices.label: The whole file, because close flushes it
choices.feedback: close only releases the descriptor.

choices.label: The file name but no data
choices.feedback: Both the data and the directory entry may be missing.

interactive.reveal: Call fsync on the file (and its directory, for a new file) before saying “saved”.

title: Signals, Exit Codes and Graceful Shutdown
objectives: Know what SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGKILL do
Shut a server down without dropping requests
Read exit codes when a process dies

cards.title: Signals are asynchronous notifications
cards.body: The kernel or another process can send a signal to a process: SIGINT when you press Ctrl+C, SIGTERM as a polite request to stop, SIGKILL to end it immediately. Most signals can be caught by a handler; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot.

cards.title: Graceful shutdown in four steps
cards.body: On SIGTERM a server should stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, flush buffers and close connections to databases and queues, then exit with status 0. Orchestrators wait a grace period, then send SIGKILL.

cards.title: Worked example: a rolling deploy without errors
cards.body: An orchestrator replaces a pod while it still holds requests.
steps: The pod is removed from load-balancer endpoints and receives SIGTERM, roughly at the same time
The server keeps serving for a few seconds so traffic still routed to it is not refused
It stops accepting new connections and finishes in-flight requests, bounded by a deadline under the grace period (30 s by default in Kubernetes)
It closes pools and exits 0
Without this, every deploy drops the requests that were in flight

cards.title: Misconception: the process will get a chance to clean up
cards.body: SIGKILL ends a process without running any code, and power loss or an OOM kill do the same. Graceful shutdown handles the planned case; data integrity must still survive the unplanned one, through transactions, idempotent work and durable logs.

cards.title: Trap: the main process does not receive the signal
cards.body: If a container starts the server through a shell script, the shell may be process 1 and not forward SIGTERM to its child. The server never sees the signal and is killed after the grace period. Even when the server itself is PID 1, the kernel applies no default action to signals it has not handled, so it must install its own SIGTERM handler. Use exec to replace the shell, or a small init process that forwards signals.

cards.title: Edge case: PID 1 must reap orphaned children
cards.body: When a process exits, it stays a zombie holding a process-table entry until its parent collects its exit status with wait. Orphans are re-parented to PID 1. An application running as PID 1 that never calls wait collects zombies from every helper its children leave behind, until the container’s process limit is reached and new processes cannot start. A minimal init such as tini forwards signals and reaps zombies, so the application does not have to.

questions.prompt: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?

choices.label: SIGHUP
SIGKILL
SIGINT
SIGTERM

questions.explanation: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) bypass handlers.

questions.prompt: What should a server do first on SIGTERM?

choices.label: Restart itself in place
Exit immediately with status 0
Stop taking new work, finish in-flight
Wait for a second SIGTERM

questions.explanation: Draining keeps requests from being dropped.

questions.prompt: A container exits with code 137. What does that usually mean?

choices.label: It failed to start because of a syntax error
It exited normally after a clean shutdown
It was killed by signal 9, SIGKILL
It received SIGTERM and handled it

questions.explanation: Shells and runtimes report death by signal as 128 plus the signal number, and 137 − 128 = 9 is SIGKILL, commonly from an out-of-memory kill or a grace period running out. A start-up error usually exits with a small code such as 1 or 2, a clean exit is 0, and a handled SIGTERM normally ends with the program’s own code (often 0, or 143 if it re-raises SIGTERM).

questions.prompt: A server started by a shell script never logs “shutting down” on deploy. Likely cause?

choices.label: The log buffer is too small
SIGTERM is not sent to containers
The shell does not forward SIGTERM
Deploys always use SIGKILL

questions.explanation: With a shell as PID 1, SIGTERM reaches the shell, which does not pass it on, so the server never starts shutting down and is killed when the grace period ends. Platforms send SIGTERM first and SIGKILL only after the grace period, containers receive signals like any other process, and the log buffer size does not stop a message being written.

questions.prompt: Order a graceful shutdown.

items.label: Finish in-flight requests within a deadline
Exit with status 0
Stop accepting new connections
Close database and queue connections
Receive SIGTERM

questions.explanation: Drain, then release, then exit.

questions.prompt: A process is killed by signal 15 (SIGTERM) without handling it. What exit status does the shell report?
assumptions: Shell convention: 128 + signal number
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 143 means the process was terminated before it could exit on its own, so a graceful handler was missing or never ran.

flashcards.back: SIGTERM asks to stop and can be handled; SIGKILL ends the process at once.
128 + 9: killed by SIGKILL, often OOM or grace expiry.
Stop new work, drain in-flight, release resources, exit 0.

mechanism.title: How processes are told to stop
steps: Each signal has a default action: terminate, terminate with a core dump, ignore, stop or continue. A process can install handlers for most signals; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP always take their default action.

Handlers run asynchronously, interrupting whatever the thread was doing, so only async-signal-safe functions may be called in them. The usual pattern is to set a flag or write to a pipe in the handler and do the real shutdown in normal code.

Process 1 in a container (or on a host) is special: the kernel does not apply default terminate actions to it for signals it has not installed handlers for. A server running as process 1 without a SIGTERM handler may therefore ignore SIGTERM entirely.

Kubernetes termination: the pod is marked terminating, removed from Service endpoints, any preStop hook runs, SIGTERM is sent, and after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) remaining processes get SIGKILL. Endpoint removal propagates asynchronously, which is why servers keep serving briefly after SIGTERM.

Exit status: 0 means success, other small numbers are program-defined errors, and shells and orchestrators report death by signal as 128 + the signal number (130 for SIGINT, 137 for SIGKILL, 143 for SIGTERM).

Disposability (a twelve-factor principle) asks that processes start fast and shut down gracefully, and that work survives sudden death: jobs are returned to a queue if a worker dies, and requests are idempotent so clients can retry.

useWhen: Use a SIGTERM handler that drains connections within a deadline.
Use exec or a minimal init so the server receives signals in containers.
avoidWhen: Avoid long or unsafe work inside signal handlers.
Avoid relying on shutdown hooks for correctness; SIGKILL and crashes skip them.

rows: Orchestrator or kill command asking to stop
Grace period expired, OOM killer, kill -9
Terminal closed; often reused to reload config

numbers.title: Fitting a drain into the grace period
assumptions: Grace period 30 s (Kubernetes default); endpoint removal takes up to 5 s to propagate (illustrative)
The slowest normal request takes 10 s; closing pools and flushing takes 2 s
steps: Keep serving for about 5 s after SIGTERM so late-routed requests still succeed.
Then stop accepting and let in-flight requests finish: up to 10 s.
Then close pools and flush: 2 s. Total ≈ 17 s, inside 30 s.
Set an internal deadline (say 25 s) after which remaining requests are cancelled, so the process exits before SIGKILL.
numbers.result: Budget the shutdown explicitly; anything not finished by the grace period is killed mid-flight.

india.title: Pod termination in the Kubernetes documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes Pod lifecycle documentation describes the termination sequence: the pod is marked for deletion, endpoints stop including it, the preStop hook runs, the container runtime sends SIGTERM to process 1 in each container, and after the grace period (30 seconds by default) any remaining processes receive SIGKILL. It also notes that endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so a server should expect a few late requests after the signal arrives.

pitfalls.trap: “We handle shutdown, so no data can be lost.”
pitfalls.say: “Only on SIGTERM; SIGKILL, OOM and power loss skip it, so the work itself must be idempotent and durable.”

pitfalls.trap: “Exit code 137 means our code crashed.”
pitfalls.say: “137 is SIGKILL, usually the OOM killer or an expired grace period; check memory limits and shutdown time.”

takeaways: SIGTERM can be handled; SIGKILL cannot.
Graceful shutdown: keep serving briefly, drain, release, exit 0.
Exit status 128 + n means death by signal n.
Make sure the server, not a wrapper shell, receives signals.

interactive.title: What happens on deploy?
interactive.prompt: A container runs “sh -c ./server”. The server has a SIGTERM handler that drains requests. Kubernetes deletes the pod with the default grace period.

choices.label: The shell gets SIGTERM, the server never does, and both are SIGKILLed after 30 s
choices.feedback: Right: the shell is process 1 and does not forward the signal by default.

choices.label: The server drains and exits 0
choices.feedback: Only if it receives SIGTERM, which it does not here.

choices.label: The pod is removed instantly with no wait
choices.feedback: Kubernetes waits the grace period before SIGKILL.

interactive.reveal: Start the server with exec (or a tiny init) so it is the process that receives SIGTERM.
